newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian protesters raise red flags, not glasses.
newsitem.headline: Russian protesters raise red flags, not glasses.

text.p: Russia's day of protests on Thursday gave thousands of people in the heart of this pro-communist region a reason to raise their old red flags -- but no chance to buy a bottle of vodka.

Local authorities said about 90,000 people went on strike for a few hours or took part in marches in the Krasnodar region, part of the communist-dominated Red Belt, to protest against the government's economic policy and delays in payment of wages and pensions.
In the regional capital Krasnodar, the protest recalled Soviet-style May Day parades. Many in the elderly crowd appeared to be veterans of communist celebrations.

Thousands paraded with signs and flags adorned with the hammer and sickle. Others used the opportunity to go roller-skating, stroll with the dog or otherwise enjoy a sunny day on the central street closed to cars.
To assure an orderly crowd, pro-Communist governor Nikolai Kondratenko banned all alcohol sales for the day.
"If desperate people drink alcohol, misfortunes occur," he said.
The decree meant alcohol stores and many street kiosks closed shop, but factories where wages often fall behind schedule continued to work with only very limited disruptions.
But Kondratenko, who said his own wages were about two months behind schedule, gave the event one boost by ordering enterprises to let their people march.
"I agree with these people that we must change the course of reform but I cannot call people to the streets. It's alarming to me, a source of concern," he told Reuters on Thursday.
"Attention comrades," loadspeakers blared as crowds gathered in the early afternoon and a marching band played upbeat music.
Banners were more dire, declaring: "Don't let children die", "Protect the Textile Industry" and "The great Russia has been reduced to poverty!"
Others tried a wry approach, criticising Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, father of Russia's privatisation program. "I'd swap a Chubais for a sausage," read one sign.
In a region which initially voted overwhelmingly for the communist presidential candidate in 1996, the turnout was lower than unions had hoped. This reflected a nationwide trend.
"Public apathy is very high. People don't believe this will lead to anything," said Yuri Zaleski, a taxi driver.

Union officials had hoped to attract 25,000 people, or about five percent of the city population, and said even more showed up. But the regional government said 12,000 had turned out, and others said the numbers were closer to 6,000.
Deputy governor Nikolai Kharchenko said the low turnout in Krasnodar was the result of the spring sowing season.
"We have a saying -- if you don't plant on time, you don't put food on the table," he said.
Many protesters were studies in Russian resourcefulness.

"I haven't been paid my salary of 330,000 roubles in three months," said Pyotr Berezin, a biologist who inspects fish processing plants. "For three months my wife and I have lived off the pensions of my parents and in-laws."

Oleg Shenyak, 30, a nurse whose salary of about the same amount comes about a month late, said he lives with his wife in a small room outside the city. Their daughter lives with her grandmother because they do not have enough room for her.
